synopsis: Across chapters, false confidence arises when plausible or repeatable simulation results exceed their evidence: millions of tests cannot establish operating-domain coverage, and statistical methods cannot repair missing hazards or an unvalidated simulator [f671, f650, f8916]. Extrapolation is a central warning: Columbia was lost in 2003 partly because a model was used outside its validity envelope, with debris estimated at about 400 times the size represented in its test database (640 times in an early briefing); even a well-calibrated braking model may fail on downhill or different-load conditions [f11326, f7582, f6171]. Metrics can conceal error: a 2021 radar study found deceptively realistic tracking despite the largest raw-point-cloud gap, while CVPR 2024 on-road research showed that open-loop planning metrics could be matched using vehicle state alone [f4540, f5518]. Test design also matters: incorrect scenario distributions invalidate sampling-based performance claims, correlated frames artificially narrow confidence intervals, and shared assumptions across sensors, collision logic and the pass/fail oracle can produce consistent but misleading results [f6833, f5461, f12118]. These risks extend beyond sensors to site generation, terrain physics and human response: generators may omit failure-generating structure, common handling tire models do not work on deformable terrain, and on-road warning-system benefit estimates ranged from 53% to 96% with the chosen driver model [f3736, f8339, f3045]. Planning should therefore avoid blanket validation claims, review oracle independence, and separate replay, post-intervention simulation and real-machine stopping evidence; the proposing organization has not yet validated its simulator against reality, leaving replacement of physical evidence unjustified [f9762, f10233, f5551, f10475].
